items.title: From food to fuel, AI helps pinpoint how to grow 'microalgae' at scale
items.excerpt: Microalgae (microscopic organisms that use light and carbon dioxide to grow) can be used to make ingredients and food for animals, pigments and potentially renewable fuels. But growing microalgae efficiently at an industrial scale is difficult.

items.title: Can scientists build a lie detector for AI chatbots?
items.excerpt: Ask an AI chatbot for some medical advice and it might recommend you head to the hospital when all you really have is indigestion. One of the biggest issues with AI chatbots today is that they can still share false information, according to Northeastern experts.

items.title: Does the gender pay gap extend to AI? Research finds female AI agents 'paid' less
items.excerpt: New research from the University of Limerick has found that gender bias in the workplace could be replicated in interactions with artificial intelligence.

items.title: AI may help catch heart transplant rejection without biopsies
items.excerpt: By analyzing heart rhythm recordings and blood tests, artificial intelligence may accurately flag when a transplant patient's body starts attacking a donated heart, a new study suggests.

items.title: Is AI the End of Math As We Know It?
items.excerpt: Mathematicians are facing the sudden shift with grief, anger, and a desperate search for fresh ideas: “If we don’t adapt, there’s just no more math in 50 years.”

items.title: Supercomputing researchers document evolution of AI hardware
items.excerpt: Since 2018, the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center has maintained a survey of the latest AI hardware to help researchers and the U.S. government gain a better understanding of the AI accelerator landscape and make better research and acquisition decisions about them.

items.title: The effects of an “algorithmic monoculture” depend on the details
items.excerpt: The use of a single hiring algorithm by multiple firms, known as algorithmic monoculture, is less problematic for job seekers than past research has shown, and may even be a good thing depending on the approach used, according to a study by MIT researchers.

items.title: The promise and peril of using visual AI to study cities
items.excerpt: In the book “How AI Sees the City,” MIT researchers examine implications of using visual AI to study urban life. Across cities, more images means more data, more insight — and more concerns about privacy and fairness.
